content: Pressure ulcers, also known as bedsores, affect approximately 10% of hospitalized patients, with elderly individuals being at the highest risk. Some studies have proposed that massage therapy might help prevent the development of pressure ulcers, but the findings from these studies are inconsistent. The objective of this review was to evaluate the evidence regarding the effects of massage therapy compared to placebo, standard care, or other interventions in preventing pressure ulcers in populations at risk. Specifically, the review aimed to address the following questions: Does massage therapy reduce the incidence of pressure ulcers of any grade? Is massage therapy safe in both the short and long term? If it is not safe, what adverse events are associated with its use? To answer these questions, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL. The search covered studies up to January 8, 2015, and no restrictions were applied regarding the date or language of publication. The review intended to include all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials (Q-RCTs) that assessed the effects of massage therapy for preventing pressure ulcers. The primary outcome of interest was the proportion of individuals who developed a new pressure ulcer of any grade. Two independent reviewers screened the studies for inclusion, and any disagreements were resolved through discussion. However, no studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. As a result, it was not possible to perform a meta-analysis or provide a narrative synthesis of the evidence. The authors concluded that there are currently no eligible studies available to determine whether massage therapy is effective in preventing pressure ulcers. Consequently, the effectiveness and safety of massage therapy for this purpose remain unclear.
